To purse means to press your lips together tightly so that they form a small, puckered, rounded shape — almost like a tiny knot or a small "o" pulled inward. Think of how a drawstring bag closes when you pull the strings: the opening gathers, tightens, and puckers into a small, bunched circle. When you purse your lips, your mouth does exactly that.

This verb is almost always used with the word lips as its object. You will almost never see "purse" used as a verb without lips being involved.

Picture someone who has just tasted something unpleasant, or someone who is trying very hard not to say what they're thinking. Their lips press together, squeeze inward slightly, and form a tight little round shape — not quite a smile, not quite a frown, but a firm, compact expression. That is pursed lips.

This is where the word gets really interesting and useful. People purse their lips for several reasons, and a good writer or speaker uses this word deliberately because it carries emotional meaning:

Disapproval or annoyance — This is the most common one. When someone hears something they don't like or disagrees strongly, they may purse their lips instead of speaking. It signals silent judgment.

Holding something back — A person might purse their lips to stop themselves from laughing, from crying, or from saying something they shouldn't. The tightness of the lips physically holds things in.

Concentration or deep thought — Sometimes people purse their lips when they are thinking hard about something, especially when working through a difficult decision.

Skepticism or doubt — When someone is not convinced by what you've just said, pursed lips can signal "I'm not sure I believe you."

"Purse" is a transitive verb, meaning it needs an object — and that object is almost always lips. The structure is simple:

  • Subject + pursed + his/her/their lips

It's most often used in the past tense because writers use it to describe a character's reaction in a moment:

"She pursed her lips."

You can also use it as a present participle to show an ongoing action or to modify a noun:

"He sat there, pursing his lips thoughtfully."
"She gave him a pursing-lips kind of look." (informal, rare)

Here are clear, natural examples so you can see the word in action:

  • "The teacher pursed her lips when she saw the messy classroom." — She was displeased but didn't say anything.
  • "He pursed his lips, staring at the math problem for a long time." — Deep concentration.
  • "She pursed her lips to keep from laughing out loud." — Holding back laughter.
  • "My mother pursed her lips when I told her my plan." — Quiet disapproval.
  • "The doctor pursed her lips and nodded slowly before delivering the news." — Thoughtfulness mixed with seriousness.

When you see "pursed lips" in a book or hear someone describe an expression this way, know that it is rarely neutral. Pursed lips almost always mean that a person is feeling something strongly but choosing not to say it outright — whether that's annoyance, doubt, amusement, or deep thought. It is the face of someone holding something inside.

That's the full picture of "purse" as a verb: a tight, puckered pressing of the lips together, loaded with quiet but unmistakable emotion.
